bracket: [Textbook misprint, corrected above: the printed final value is \(1.05 \times 10^{20}\,\text{A m}^{2}\), which is a thousand times too small and is refuted by the example's OWN preceding line. That line reads \(4\times 10^{-5} \times (6.4\times 10^{6})^{3} \times 10^{7}\), and \((6.4\times 10^{6})^{3} = 2.62144\times 10^{20}\), so the product is \(1.0486\times 10^{23}\). The mantissa 1.05 is therefore correct and only the exponent is wrong — 20 printed for 23. The corrected value is also the physically right order of magnitude: the Earth's magnetic dipole moment is about \(8\times 10^{22}\,\text{A m}^{2}\), whereas \(10^{20}\) would make the Earth a thousand times weaker than it is.]

[Textbook misprint in the theory this question examines: section 12.5 defines the geographic meridian as "a plane perpendicular to the surface of the Earth (vertical plane) perpendicular to geographic axis". "Perpendicular to" should read "passing through". A plane perpendicular to the geographic axis is the equatorial plane, which is not vertical and is not a meridian at all, so the printed definition is self-contradictory. Three parts of the book itself give the correct form: the magnetic meridian is defined one line below as a vertical plane "passing through the magnetic axis"; Fig. 12.6 draws the geographic meridian as a vertical plane containing the geographic North-South line; and this chapter's own Exercise Q.1 (ii) offers "passing through the geographic axis" as the geographic-meridian alternative. Declination, defined as the angle between the two meridians, would also be meaningless if one of them were the equatorial plane. The answer above uses the corrected definition.]
